title: BMS meets the Education Minister on mid-day meal workers
author: Editorial Desk
summary: A BMS delegation met Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in September 2025 on mid-day meal workers: the memorandum, the Rs 10,000 honorarium demand and the response.
body:
*Photo: BMS delegation with the Union Education Minister, September 2025*

In early September 2025, a delegation of the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh met the **Union Education Minister, Shri Dharmendra Pradhan**, and submitted a memorandum on the problems of **mid-day meal workers** across the country. The delegation was led by B. Surendran, the All-India Organising Secretary, and Ashok Shukla, an All-India Secretary, according to a report published on the BMS website on 5 September 2025. This post explains who these workers are, what the memorandum said, how the minister responded and what happens next.

## Who the workers are

Every school day, millions of children in government and government-aided schools are served a hot meal. The scheme began in 1995 as the National Programme of Nutritional Support to Primary Education, and it became a legal entitlement after the Supreme Court, in an order of 28 November 2001 in the right-to-food case brought by the People's Union for Civil Liberties, directed that cooked meals be provided in government and government-assisted primary schools. In 2021 it was renamed **PM POSHAN**. According to Wikipedia, it covers about 120 million children in more than 1.27 million schools, and over 2.5 million cooks-cum-helpers prepare the meals.

The Ministry of Education runs the scheme, and its cost is shared between the Centre and the States. Wikipedia gives the sharing pattern as 60 per cent from the Centre and 40 per cent from the States, with States often contributing more. The honorarium of the cooks and helpers is part of that shared arrangement, which is why a request on pay reaches both the Union Minister and the State governments.

The work is cooking, serving and cleaning for large numbers of children every school day. The status of those who do it is unusual. They are not regular government employees, and they are described in official papers as workers engaged on an honorarium and not as employees.

## What the delegation raised

According to the BMS report, the memorandum covered these issues:

- **Low honorarium.** BMS stated that it has demanded a monthly honorarium of Rs 10,000.
- **Work outside the role.** Workers are often made to do jobs besides cooking, such as sweeping the school, acting as watchmen or office boys.
- **Insufficient rations.** In many States, district officials do not provide sufficient rations for the number of students.
- **Delayed reimbursement.** In Madhya Pradesh, Self-Help Groups were assigned the work, but their expenses are not reimbursed, so the women wait months for payment.
- **Health facilities and harassment.** The broader complaints include inadequate health facilities and harassment by supervisory staff and the district administration.

Each of these is a practical problem and not just a slogan. A cook who must buy supplies on credit because rations have not arrived is paying for the scheme from her own pocket. A woman who is asked to sweep classrooms and guard the gate has, in effect, been given extra jobs for the same honorarium. And an honorarium that is paid after months of delay is very difficult to live on.

## The demonstrations that preceded it

The meeting was not the beginning of the campaign. The BMS report says that on **1 July** the Akhil Bharatiya Mid-Day Meal Karmachari Mahasangh, a BMS unit, held demonstrations at around 400 locations and sent a memorandum to the Prime Minister and the Education Minister. The meeting with Shri Pradhan followed, as part of the same line of action.

## The minister's response

According to the BMS report, the minister responded positively. He promised to write to the Finance Minister about raising the monthly wages, and to arrange an official meeting soon with the concerned officials. BMS thanked him for hearing the delegation. The report also says that the minister responded to the issues on his social media accounts.

These are commitments to correspond and to meet and not decisions on pay. The honorarium is part of a scheme whose cost is shared between the Centre and the States, so any increase requires the approval of the Finance Ministry and the participation of the States. That is why the minister's promise to write to the Finance Minister is the step that matters.

## The BMS method

The BMS pattern in such cases is to meet the minister concerned, submit a written memorandum with facts, follow up by letter, and raise the question in tripartite and consultative forums. It then keeps the issue alive through its federations in the States, which can press State governments on the part of the cost they bear. The demonstrations of 1 July and the delegation of September were two stages of that pattern.

It is also typical of BMS that it combines dialogue with public pressure. The Organiser describes the BMS approach as solutions through struggle and dialogue, and the mid-day meal campaign fits it: a nationwide day of demonstrations, followed by a meeting and a memorandum.

## What workers hope for

As in earlier posts on this blog, the demands associated with mid-day meal workers include:

- a **higher honorarium** moving towards a minimum wage, with Rs 10,000 a month being BMS's stated figure;
- payment for the **full year**, and prompt payment each month;
- **social security** and pension, since a worker who has cooked for twenty years may retire with nothing;
- **safe cooking conditions** and insurance against burns and accidents; and
- relief from **non-cooking duties** and from harassment.

The new Labour Codes, in force from 21 November 2025, extend social security to categories of workers that were previously left out, and unions of scheme workers will be watching to see whether that extends to them in practice.

## What readers can do

If you know a cook in your child's school, ask her what she is paid, how often, and whether the rations arrive on time. That conversation is where most reforms start. It would also help to remember that a school meal is only as good as the person who cooks it: when we speak about nutrition, the working conditions of the cook are part of the subject.
